summary: Collects the common practice of using alias names in DNS, such as CNAMEs, for services like FTP and web servers, for example naming the web server www. It also proposes how to handle names for new protocols. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Companies give their web or file computers easy nicknames. This writes down the common nicknames and how to choose new ones, so moving a service does not break anything.

questions: why is the web server called www
what are common dns alias names for services
does a www dns entry mean a web server exists
cname vs a record for service aliases
subtitle: Why the web server is called www: the folklore of service nicknames in DNS, written down as a best current practice.

tldr.problem: Organizations name their FTP, Gopher and web servers with alias names in the DNS, but no document listed these common names, and programs had no reliable way to discover which services a site runs.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC gathers the existing naming conventions into one table of standard aliases such as www, ftp and mail, and says that new protocols must propose their own name.
tldr.outcome: The aliases are only hints, not a registration of a service. The RFC itself points to DNS SRV records as the longer-term answer.

today: RFC 2219 is a Best Current Practice, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text itself calls the conventions a short-term measure and points to DNS SRV records (RFC 2052) as the longer-term approach.

sections.title: Why Service Aliases Exist
sections.content:
To find the network services at a domain, you could search centralized databases such as Web or Usenet News "wanderers", or guess from whatever DNS information is available. The first approach is not practical when the one asking is a program.

The best-known example of guessing is the web: people try adding http://www. in front of an organization's domain name, for instance turning hivnet.fr into http://www.hivnet.fr. Some popular browsers even did this expansion automatically.

The DNS already answers some questions directly: MX records say how mail is routed, SOA records say who is responsible for a domain, and NS records say which hosts provide name service. For everything else, a CNAME or A record pointing at the host that provides the service is by far the most common convention, and this RFC formalizes it slightly.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want to find a company's website, you can guess that it starts with www. This RFC says that guess is a good habit and writes it down.

sections.title: The Generic Framework
sections.content:
The approach is simple. The RFC defines a standard set of DNS aliases for the most popular network services of the time. For a protocol that is not listed, the protocol's own specification must propose a name.

The abstract gives two reasons this is useful: it lets a service move from one machine to another transparently, and it lets people or agents discover programmatically that an organization runs, say, a World-Wide Web server.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one list of standard nicknames. If your new gadget is not on the list, whoever invents it picks a nickname and writes it in their rules.

sections.title: The Standard Alias Names
sections.content:
Section 3 lists the special cases, each alias paired with the service and the document that defines it. Among them: www for World-Wide Web HTTP, ftp for the File Transfer Protocol, mail for SMTP mail, news for Usenet News via NNTP, pop for the Post Office Protocol, ntp for the Network Time Protocol, ldap for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol and whois for NICNAME/WHOIS.

The full table also covers archie, finger, gopher, ph (the CCSO nameserver), rwhois and wais.

The CCSO nameserver had at least three aliases in common use: ph, cso and ns. Because ns is mostly used to name DNS servers, the RFC suggests ph. Sites that already use the others may keep all three, which makes the service easier to find.
sections.plainLanguage: The list says: call your web computer www, your file computer ftp, your mail computer mail. When two nicknames clash, the RFC picks one.

sections.title: Setting Up the DNS Entries
sections.content:
Domain administrators are encouraged to use these names for the services they run. It makes it easier for outsiders to find information about the organization and easier to move a service between machines.

There are two conventional ways to create the entries. One is a single CNAME record, for example ph.hivnet.fr. IN CNAME baby.hivnet.fr.. In that case nothing else may exist for that name in the DNS; it could not also have an MX record. The other is an A record for each IP address of the name, for example ph.hivnet.fr. IN A 194.167.157.2.

The RFC does not simply recommend CNAMEs over A records, since each site has its own requirements. It points to RFC 1912 for the configuration issues of CNAMEs.

Some DNS servers offer "round-robin", returning a host's addresses in a different order each time. Some clients pick among several addresses by heuristics such as the shortest round-trip time. If a server is mirrored, it may then be useful to list the mirrors' addresses as A records of the primary server, but only when the mirrors are exact copies.
sections.plainLanguage: You can either say "this nickname is just another name for that computer" or give the nickname its own address. Either works, and the best choice depends on your setup.

sections.title: Hints, Not Registrations
sections.content:
The widespread aliases make it sometimes possible to guess an organization's service names, though this gets harder as more organizations register names. Implementors must understand that a DNS entry such as www.hivnet.fr is not a registration of a web service. The name need not resolve to an address, a host need not be listening, a server need not use port 80, and even if all of that is true there is no guarantee it will honor requests from arbitrary clients. The RFC asks that the aliases be taken as useful hints and that implementations be resilient when a name does not point to the expected service.

There are also limits. Some services need more than a server name. An LDAP client, for example, needs a starting search base within the Directory Information Tree, and this document does not address that. The conventions are also only useful once the organization's domain name is known.
sections.plainLanguage: A nickname is only a hint. Just because a door is labeled "www" does not mean anybody is home.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The DNS is open to many kinds of spoofing attacks, so a lookup result cannot be guaranteed to be genuine. Spoofing can be a denial of service, such as sending a client to a non-existent address, or a passive attack, such as an intruder's server that masquerades as the legitimate one.

The RFC notes that work was ongoing on DNS security (RFC 2065). Meanwhile, stronger authentication such as public key cryptography with large key sizes is a prerequisite when the DNS is used in sensitive situations such as online financial transactions or querying medical records. Strong encryption of the network traffic may also be advisable against TCP connection hijacking and packet sniffing.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could trick the phone book into sending you to the wrong place, so for important things like money you need extra locks.
